name: Access for Every Student
title: Access for Every Student
answer: Access for Every Student means using AI to make social studies content reachable for every learner, including students reading below grade level, English learners, and students with disabilities. It matters because the same difficult texts that carry the curriculum can otherwise shut students out of discussions and thinking. The supports are meant to open the content, never to do the thinking for the student.

crumbs.name: Social Studies, Civics, and World Languages

sections.body: Social studies reading is often the hardest students meet, with long sentences, unfamiliar names, and abstract ideas. The leveled text approach lets a teacher hand out the same article, such as one on the causes of a war, at several reading levels while keeping and explaining key terms. The teacher then checks that the simpler versions did not blur important distinctions between causes, events, and consequences. English learners need both language and background knowledge, so AI can build short picture glossaries for terms like democracy, tariff, or migration and translate them into home languages. Background summaries help students who did not grow up with the history being taught, so these supports let students join discussions instead of watching from the edge.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In social studies classrooms the leveled text approach gives every student the same article at a reading level they can handle, with key terms preserved and explained. For English learners, teachers can use AI to create short glossaries with pictures for terms such as democracy, tariff, or migration and translate them into students' home languages, and background summaries can fill gaps for students unfamiliar with the history. Students with disabilities use the same tools as in other subjects, including text to speech through Microsoft Immersive Reader to read documents aloud and AI generated graphic organizers to sort causes and effects. The individualized education program team decides which supports fit each student. The text does not give separate grade band guidance beyond these examples.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or finding for this idea, so it rests on practice rather than research. The chapter presents the leveled text approach as carried over from Chapter 6 and describes classroom uses such as glossaries, translations, background summaries, text to speech, and graphic organizers without citing evidence. The only check named is the teacher's own review that simpler versions did not blur important distinctions between causes, events, and consequences.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher must check that simpler versions of a text did not blur important distinctions between causes, events, and consequences. The individualized education program team, not the technology, decides which supports fit each student. Every support should open the content and not replace the thinking, so the tools are aids to access rather than substitutes for student reasoning.
